**Vignette: Minh**

Minh is a 31-year-old Vietnamese-Australian man who works as a carpenter and lives with his wife in a mid-sized city. He is soft-spoken and deliberate in conversation, choosing his words carefully, often pausing to look at his hands before he speaks. He came to therapy at his wife's urging, after months of what he describes as "just not being right."

Two years ago, Minh was stopped by police while driving home from a late job site. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated rapidly. He was pulled from his vehicle, forced to the ground, and restrained with significant force while officers shouted at him. He recalls the weight on his back, the cold of the asphalt against his cheek, and the certainty — sharp and absolute — that he was going to die. He was held for over an hour before being released without charge. No explanation was given. He drove himself home, washed his face, and told his wife he was tired.

He did not speak about it for weeks. He returned to work because he had contracts to finish and a mortgage to pay, and because staying busy felt like the only way to keep the images from settling. On the job site, he is skilled and respected — his hands know what to do even when his mind is elsewhere. But his colleagues have noticed that he flinches when someone approaches him from behind, and that he has stopped parking in the street, choosing instead to walk longer distances from car parks where he feels less exposed.

Driving is now a source of dread. He takes back roads, avoids certain intersections, and has twice turned around mid-journey when he spotted a police vehicle in traffic. His wife has quietly started driving them to family gatherings because she understands, without him having said much, that the freeway is no longer something he can manage easily.

At night, Minh sleeps poorly. He wakes in the early hours with his heart already racing, the details of that night vivid and immediate — the shouting, the pressure on his spine, the gravel under his palms. He does not always know where he is for the first few seconds. He has begun sleeping closer to the edge of the bed, near the door, and he cannot fully explain why. His wife reaches for him and he tries to stay present, but there is a distance in him now that neither of them knows how to name.

During the day he moves through a kind of low-grade vigilance that exhausts him by evening. He scans rooms when he enters them. He notices uniforms. He is short-tempered in ways that shame him — he raised his voice at a young apprentice last month over something minor and spent the rest of the day sick with guilt. He describes himself as "not the person I was," and says this with a flatness that suggests he has grown used to the loss, even if he has not accepted it.

He carries a particular grief about what the incident has done to his sense of belonging. He was born in Australia, has lived here his whole life, and had never before felt his body to be something that could be treated as a threat. That certainty — that quiet, unexamined safety — is gone now, and he is not sure it can be recovered. He wonders sometimes, while planing timber or fitting a joint, whether the feeling of being unmade in that moment on the road is something that will simply be part of him now, worked into the grain of who he is like a knot in the wood — present, structural, impossible to cut out without weakening everything around it.

He is here, he says, because his wife asked him to come. But also, he admits after a long pause, because he is tired of being afraid of his own country.
